As Featured In & Supported By

"Each piece is a thread in the larger
fabric of Ilonggo resilience."

Mann Cayona begins with two finished oil paintings. Each is cut by hand into long vertical or horizontal strips — then rewoven, one over, one under, until both canvases become a single, unified surface. The technique echoes the loom traditions of Panay Island: the hablon of Miagao and Oton, the patadyong wrap-cloth of the Ilonggo coast — textiles that carry memory in every interlace. What emerges is neither the first painting nor the second, but a third thing entirely: a conversation between images, a collision of worlds.

About the Artist

The
Weave

Mann Cayona is a self-taught oil painter based in Iloilo City, Philippines, working out of a small home studio in Tigbauan. What began as straightforward portraiture has evolved into a signature process: cutting each finished painting into strips — sometimes as narrow as a centimeter — then reweaving them entirely by hand. Over, under. Over, under. The rhythm is meditative, unforgiving, irreversible.

Two paintings become one surface. Two histories, two palettes, two moments in time, interlaced into a single object. The gaps between strips are left visible — the silence between notes that makes music possible.

On Panay Island, weaving is a livelihood and a lineage: the loom keeps time, the thread carries ancestry. Cayona transposes that logic onto oil on canvas — a material conversation between the Old Masters and the barangay, between Caravaggio and the hablon weavers of Miagao, between memory and survival. The work has since been shown at local exhibitions and open-air fairs around Iloilo, and covered by regional press and broadcast media.
